films.title: Wu Ming Nü Hai
films.logline: Play Trailer Born in the wake of China’s controversial one-child policy, six-year-old Wang Juan (Cao Ruofan) finds her life completely upended by her mother’s pregnancy. The young girl is soon taken from her rural home—where kite-flying and swimming fill her days—and brought to the home of a discordant, childless couple. Abandoned in an unfamiliar city with her new legal guardians, Juan strives to find a sense of belonging, a struggle that only worsens when she’s uprooted twice more before turning 18 years old. Anchored by a powerful performance from Resurrection’s Li Gengxi, who plays teenage Juan, Zou Jing’s confident debut is an achingly tender coming-of-age drama. And while it never shies away from the harrowing realities of the political directive that dehumanized and haunted so many, A Girl Unknown also reaffirms the undeniable, striking hopefulness of a young person’s belief in love and self. —Kate Bove

films.title: A Long Winter
films.logline: With an intimate tale of tender heartbreak, 45 Years (MVFF38) and All of Us Strangers filmmaker Andrew Haigh transports his observant temperament and distinctive lens into the unsteadiness of domestic life to the Mountain West of the early 1950s. Based on a short story by Colm Tóibín, a perfect literary match for Haigh’s melancholic rhythms, A Long Winter follows young Mike (Fred Hechinger, with his finest turn in a rapidly bourgeoning career) and his resolute father (Ebon Moss-Bachrach) in the overwhelming aftermath of Mike’s brother leaving for the Korean War, and his mother (Caitríona Balfe) disappearing in a snow storm. While the icy temperatures settle in across an increasingly fruitless search, something slowly begins to thaw within Mike as he becomes aware of his own passions and sexual longings. Juxtaposed against the relentless majesty of snow-clad heights, Haigh’s painterly interiors and soulful depths gorgeously articulate repressed, unspoken emotions that refuse to continue hibernating. —Tomris Laffly
films.producers: Andrew Haigh, Chad Oakes, Michael Elliott, Mike Frislev, Tristan Goligher

films.title: A Prayer for the Dying
films.logline: Play Trailer Dara Van Dusen’s feature debut is a visually compelling Western set in 1870 in Friendship, Wisconsin. In the settlement—a place with not much more than a general store, a church, and a handful of smallholdings—everyone ekes out the barest of existences, including Jacob (Johnny Flynn), the town’s sheriff, preacher, and undertaker. When an outbreak of diphtheria threatens the community’s stability, he and the village doctor (John C. Reilly) navigate the threat as best they know how: initially, by concealing it, hoping it will subside. But Jacob finds himself torn between his roles as a leader, a husband and father, and a Civil War veteran navigating the haunting memories of his service, as another threat, a wildfire, looms on the horizon. With striking cinematography and sound design, Van Dusen creates a world both familiar and eerily apocalyptic, driven by great central performances. It’s a notable achievement for a first-time filmmaker. —Zoë Elton
films.producers: Dyveke Bjørkly Graver

films.title: A Talent for Murder
films.logline: Play Trailer In Anton Corbijn’s playful thriller, Oscar winner Helen Mirren delivers a fiendishly juicy portrayal of the legendary mystery author Patricia Highsmith in an imaginary scenario with a wicked sense of humor. Based on Joanna Murray-Smith’s play, Switzerland (adapted for the screen by the playwright herself), the story follows the famously tough Highsmith while the retired author receives a visit from over-ambitious publishing rep Edward Ridgeway (Alden Ehrenreich, unpredictable at every turn) at her handsome Swiss Alps home. The year is 1995 and the talented Mr. Ridgeway has but one mission: convince Highsmith to conjure up a final Tom Ripley murder mystery, poised to be a bestseller. As the equally stubborn and deliberate Ridgeway and Highsmith face off across a mazy creative process where their unknowable instincts often clash, the line between reality and fiction blurs in unimaginable ways, spilling both the blood and the beans as stylishly as a Highsmith novel. —Tomris Laffly

films.title: All American Girls
films.logline: If you’ve ever pined for an American Girl doll or its tiny, perfect accessories, this documentary is right in your dollhouse. Director Christy Wegener ( I Am Vanessa Guillen ) pulls back the meticulously crafted curtain on the venture that quietly began as Pleasant Company and vaulted into the multimillion-dollar empire known as American Girl®. Featuring an exclusive interview with founder Pleasant Rowland, along with archival footage and insights from original staffers and diehard fans, this energetic deep dive examines the feminist and academic framework behind the characters and the triumphs and controversies that shaped the booming business. Get the backstory on how Rowland dreamed up the historical dolls and their intricate worlds. Meet the adults who keep aflame the passion that defined their childhoods in the ‘80s, ‘90s, and early 2000s. And revel in feisty memes and multimedia artwork that illuminate the brand’s unparalleled influence and ongoing cultural relevance. —D. Quinones

films.title: Avedon
films.logline: Academy Award®-winning director Ron Howard traces the man behind the camera and the iconic images that made Richard Avedon one of the most influential photographers of the 20th century. From the stark white backgrounds that became his signature to his unforgettable portraits of cultural icons like Charlie Chaplin and Marilyn Monroe, Avedon redefined the visual language of fashion and celebrity. Yet beyond the glamour, the film delves into a childhood home built on staged happiness, revealing how those early experiences informed his personal life and artistic vision. With unprecedented access to personal archives, home movies, never-before-seen photographs, and interviews with his son John Avedon, fashion titan Calvin Klein, art dealer Larry Gagosian, and famous muses Isabella Rossellini, Twiggy, and Lauren Hutton, Avedon offers a rare glimpse into the deeply private artist whose extraordinary body of work continues to shape the worlds of photography, fashion, and culture. —Michelle Svenson Justin Wilkes in Conversation Tuesday, October 6, 4:30 PM | SEQ 1

films.title: Bedford Park
films.logline: A car becomes the connective tissue of director Stephanie Ahn’s absorbing debut, gradually drawing two broken souls together and giving them the space to see one another. Korean American Audrey (Moon Choi) is in her 30s and obsessed with having a child. After her mother is in an auto accident, Audrey confronts Eli (Son Suk-ku), the man responsible for the crash. Ahn deftly steers the upheaval of their encounter into an increasingly intimate, if fumbling, relationship. The air between the characters is thick. The Korean concept of han waltzes across the screen with allure to spare: True sorrow outlives rage, taking the shape of endurance. With tranquil assurance, the director transforms the film’s structure and interiors into an expressive world entirely her own; simmering emotional wells that sit within each character are potent and extreme. The winner of the 2026 Sundance US Dramatic Special Jury Award for Debut Feature holds you tight and doesn't let go. —Ivonne Cotorruelo

films.title: Amarga Navidad
films.logline: Play Trailer Who owns a story when an artist turns someone else's life into fiction? And what happens when that person recognizes themselves in the work? Pedro Almodóvar ( The Room Next Door , MVFF47) returns with a playful, layered story about friendship, loss, and the slippery boundary between life and fiction. In parallel stories, Elsa, a filmmaker grieving her mother and struggling with debilitating migraines, retreats to Lanzarote, while Raúl, a celebrated filmmaker, transforms the life of his longtime collaborator Mónica into a screenplay. As fiction and reality begin to overlap, Almodóvar turns his camera toward the very act of creating, exploring memory, artistic ownership, and the complicated line between inspiration and appropriation. The director’s unmistakable visual flair is everywhere, with colors shifting between worlds and singer-songwriter Chavela Vargas's haunting music adding an emotional pulse. Full of wit, melodrama, beautiful performances, and Almodóvar's singular sensibility, Bitter Christmas is the latest invitation into the cinematic universe of one of our most beloved filmmakers. — João Federici
films.producers: Agustín Almodóvar

films.title: Boss Cat
films.logline: Play Trailer Twenty-something Sonja (Olivia Hargroder, superb in her feature film debut) is an ambitious, sassy, raging bundle of creative energy whose dreams of artistic self-expression are only matched by her desire for independence. Born with Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome), she refuses to allow biology to be her destiny and defies all obstacles—and people—that block her way. But when her mom dies, Grandma Doris has other plans for Sonja—in a board-and-care facility. Sonja's anger and grief find an empowering outlet when her friend Hakim, a Sudanese refugee, introduces her to krump street dancing. First-time director Genevieve Clay-Smith collaborated with a fully inclusive cast and crew on this funny, fiery, and family-friendly film that provides a uniquely compelling and beautiful testament to the power of resilience, independence, and love. Produced by Bus Stop Films, a company dedicated to end-to-end inclusivity in film production. —K.D. Davis Appropriate for grades 7-12 (ages 12-17)

films.title: Brave Cat
films.logline: Play Trailer Kona is a young cat who dwells in the forest with her loving mother and her wise grandma . All forest creatures live together in harmony except for the solitary human who scouts the countryside with his ill-tempered hunting dogs, capturing animals for a traveling circus. When he snares her mom, Kona embarks on a quest that takes her through the forest, over snowy mountains, and down to the ocean’s shore on a quest to find her parent. While she begins her journey alone, she soon finds help and companionship from Colin, an adorable—if pesty—pup, and brave Bernard, a runaway circus bear. Oscar®-winning Chilean animator Gabriel Osorio’s beautifully imaginative settings (inspired by the Patagonian landscape) and intricate handmade production design weave a family-friendly tale of bravery, determination, and forgiveness. Winner of the 2026 Annecy International Animation Film Festival Annecy Presents Audience Award. —KD Davis

films.title: Brian
films.logline: “Today is going to be a good day,” repeats Brian (rising star Ben Wang, superb) to his reflection in the mirror each morning before the usual day of disappointments and misunderstandings begins. Prone to frequent outbursts due to his mental health issues, the optimistic high-schooler and his good intentions often derail into comical calamity amidst run-ins with his brother, classmates, teachers, and therapist, who are all too familiar with his emotional flare-ups. When he accidentally self-sabotages his dreams of performing in the school play, Brian finds a new calling: running for senior class president. Armed with a sharply realized script from Late Night scribe Mike Scollins that deftly balances uproarious jokes with earned heartfelt insight, and a murderer’s row of crackling performances from some of comedy’s finest talents, director Will Ropp’s breakout hit of SXSW delivers one of the most memorable coming-of-age films in years. —Landon Zakheim

films.title: Bunker
films.logline: Play Trailer Even the most beautiful love stories can start with a misunderstanding. In Florian Zeller’s ( The Father , MVFF43) elegant psychological drama, Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz are successful professionals (architect and editor, respectively) married to their work, and to each other. Their “misunderstanding” is a story Miguel (Bardem) recounts: On their first date his allergies, mistaken by Sofia (Cruz) for tears of empathy, led to their first kiss. Misunderstandings deepen when Miguel meets a tech billionaire (Paul Dano, chillingly familiar) who wants him to design a luxury bunker in Hawai’i—a project antithetical to the ideals the couple once shared. Tensions at home escalate when the blue-collar neighbor punctures a hole in the couple’s garden wall to build a window for his own garage. With an exquisite soundtrack by Volker Bertelmann ( Conclave , MVFF47), Bunker asks us to consider the silos and walls we build, and the fears we have of knocking them down. – K.D. Davis
films.producers: Federica Sainte-Rose, Fernando Bovaira

films.title: Burgundy
films.logline: Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw are modern-day masters of creative nonfiction with their melancholic portrayals of one-of-a-kind traditions and the communities who proudly carry them. After focusing on truffle-sniffing canines and humans ( The Truffle Hunters , MVFF43), and Argentine cowboys and cowgirls ( Gaucho Gaucho , 2024), the duo turns their dreamy lens to the irresistible flavors of the Burgundy region and its colorful personalities of different socioeconomic realities. From a dapper vineyard worker with an Alain Delon flair, to a service old hand so committed to the delicious ingredients of his menu that you might just applaud his disarming theatrics, individuals that construct Burgundy’s many layers all aim to make a lasting impression like that last great bottle of wine you’ve slurped and can’t forget. A romantic cinematic journey that often winks at the pleasures and techniques of the French New Wave, Burgundy is here to caress your palate with its silky aromas and sophisticated aftertaste. —Tomris Laffly
films.producers: Cameron O’Reilly, Gregory Kershaw, Michael Dweck, Naomi Denamur

films.title: Carl Sagan: We are Made of Star Stuff
films.logline: For many, cosmologist Carl Sagan was the face of space exploration, scientific inquiry, and insatiable curiosity, his enthusiasm contagious. Nanette Burstein’s fascinating documentary reveals the man behind the legend. Sagan’s involvement in the Voyager satellite program that was instrumental not only in discovering details about Earth’s neighboring planets but also paved the way for serious discussion about extraterrestrial life catapulted the university professor and NASA advisor into the stratosphere. But with additional fame as an iconoclast (author of Cosmos , activist against nuclear proliferation) came a heavy toll: a fractured family life and difficulty adapting to his role in it, until he met his soulmate, Anne. In this absorbing evocation of Sagan’s life, Burstein employs home movies, audio archives, candid testimonials, and extraordinary space photography to tell the story of a true globalist who loved being an ambassador for the human condition, the spread of knowledge, and our relationship with the universe. —Sterling Hedgpeth

films.title: Closure
films.logline: Play Trailer Poland's Vistula River rushes along—an evocative image transformed into a visually haunting depiction of grief, encapsulating the indescribable hollowness that loss leaves behind within the living. Krzysztof was just 16 when he disappeared, last spotted by a CCTV camera as he stood on a bridge spanning the river. His father, Daniel, compulsively combs the water, refusing to give up. Following Daniel's dogged search for any trace of his missing son, the waterway becomes a space where hope and extreme grief collide. What elevates Closure is Michael Marczak's remarkable directorial precision and striking visual work, giving this nonfiction the dramatic force of a narrative film. A standout at Sundance and winner of Thessaloniki Documentary Film Festival's highest honor, the Golden Alexander, it dives deep into the shadows of the human soul with its devastating exploration of loss, becoming the cinematic equivalent of a river that flows endlessly. — Ivonne Cotorruelo

films.title: Coward
films.logline: Play Trailer In his previous films Girl (2018) and Close (2022), celebrated Belgian filmmaker Lukas Dhont explored the delicate emotional bonds between vulnerable characters. His third feature ups the stakes, bringing those concerns to the battlefield, as he focuses on two young soldiers who fall in love amidst the carnage of war. Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at the Cannes Film Festival for their unguarded portrayals of, respectively, Pierre, a shy young farmer struggling to find his voice and overcome his fear, and the proudly theatrical Francis, who spearheads a series of performances to entertain his fellow troops. This tender World War I drama subverts preconceived notions about masculinity and warfare, and Macchia (making his big-screen debut) is especially affecting as a young man who discovers an unexpected romance. Set against the brutality of combat, C oward draws inspiration from actual cross-dressing theater revues that took place during the Great War, examining how sexual identity, intimacy, and survival were interwoven during that bloody conflict. —Tim Grierson
films.producers: Michiel Dhont

films.title: Crocodile
films.logline: Hibiscus tea standing in for blood, shots of bodies vanishing from the landscape, cars that fly. The set is a small village in Kaduna, Nigeria. A group of teenagers brimming with cinephile passion plunges into a sea of adventure, creating small films that swap out their present for a future world. The village’s lack of electricity conspires against the creation of their work but doesn’t give the group dramatic pause as their films start gaining international traction and support. More than a decade since it began, the collective known as The Critics is still making films. In Crocodile , director Pietra Brettkelly alongside the Critics themselves, weaves the cinematic alchemy of a coming-of-age story with the pulse of a band of young dreamers who thread naked police brutality and a broken system into handstitched sci-fi magic. —Ivonne Cotorruelo
films.producers: Pietra Brettkelly, The Critics

films.title: Elephants in the Fog
films.logline: Play Trailer In a village in southern Nepal, Pirati is the matriarch of a Kinnar community, a third-gender tradition recognized in that country, where families form through chosen bonds of care rather than blood. When Apsara, one of Pirati’s daughters, disappears during a nightly patrol as the villagers keep watch for wild elephants, Pirati begins her own search. As the mystery opens wounds within the community, she wrestles with a difficult choice: remain with the family that gave her a home or pursue a new life with the man she loves. Around them, wild elephants move through the darkness, revered and feared, a haunting presence that echoes the film’s questions about belonging and otherness. Abinash Bikram Shah’s remarkable first feature is both a tense, immersive thriller and a tender portrait of chosen family, finding beauty in ritual, humor, desire, and everyday life. Noé Bach’s stunning cinematography makes the forest feel almost alive, while Frederic Alvarez’s haunting score draws us deeper into Pirati’s journey. Winner of the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at Cannes, Elephants in the Fog announces a filmmaker with a remarkably assured vision. —João Federici

films.title: Everest: The Other Side
films.logline: Play Trailer Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson became extreme sports stars in 2018 when they were the first to ski down Lhotse, the Everest-adjacent, fourth tallest mountain in the world. For their next challenge, the couple intended to scale Everest’s rarely attempted north face and then ski down from the summit. After a tragedy, Morrison presses on alone. His tenacity and spiritual intensity in overcoming grief, not to mention the awesome physical obstacles posed by Everest makes him one of those rare true-life adventurers whose exploits go farther than fiction. Everest: The Other Side captures Morrison’s extraordinary and risky 2025 ascent in images made all the more compelling because co-director Jimmy Chin is climbing next to Morrison, facing many of the same perils. Chin’s cinematography—along with that of Clair Popkin and Christopher Murray—and Morrison’s epic determination add up to a thrilling documentary. —Larry Gross

films.title: Everybody to Kenmure Street
films.logline: Play Trailer On the morning of Eid al-Fitr, as Muslims prepare to celebrate the end of Ramadan, tenants in a small Glasgow district notice an Immigration Enforcement van outside their windows. When two longtime neighbors are detained, text alerts set off a chain of events that quickly transforms the street into the site of an extraordinary act of solidarity. Blending crowdsourced mobile phone footage, archival material, interviews, and creative dramatizations featuring performances by Emma Thompson and Kate Dickie, the documentary captures the real-life standoff between residents and authorities. Taking on a nonconformist structure, the film conveys both the urgency of the moment and the deeper histories of migration, racism, and activism that shaped the city. At once deeply local and universally resonant, it is a testament to what can happen when a community refuses to look away. Winner of the 2026 Sundance Film Festival Special Jury Award for Civil Resistance. —Michelle Svenson
films.producers: Ciara Barry, Samuel Blanc

films.title: Everytime
films.logline: Play Trailer Austrian writer/director Sandra Wollner‘s Cannes Un Certain Regard Award winner begins with a calmly observed domestic situation. Divorced mom Ella (Minichmayr) gets ready to go on vacation while managing her squabbling daughters, teenage Jessica (Carla Hutterman) and precocious Melli (Lotte Schirin Keiling), with Jessica preferring to get high in the company of her cute boyfriend Lux (Tristán López). Before they can leave, tragedy devastates the family. A year later, the survivors take the interrupted journey to the sun-drenched Spanish resort Tenerife, and the drama becomes a unique, immersive exploration of what it means to experience grief. Woolner and her gifted cinematographer Christopher Oke (who shot 2024’s similarly themed and widely acclaimed Aftersun ) penetrate the unassuming surface of things to create a disquieting, disorienting atmosphere of dreamlike, almost Lynchian uncertainty, anchored by Minichmayr and Keiling's brilliant performances. Everytime asks us, in superbly subtle fashion, to reimagine the ways in which it is and is not possible to live through loss and resume living an everyday life. —Larry Gross
films.producers: David Bohun, Lixi Frank, Viktoria Stolpe

films.title: Extra Geography
films.logline: Play Trailer Idiosyncratic besties Flic and Minna are a pair of committed overachievers at their stately British boarding school for girls, spending their days playing lacrosse and aspiring to a pitch-perfect Oxbridge-bound future. But surely, thriving at a top university would demand one to be more “worldly”—as in, seasoned in romance. Once our novice wooers decide to practice falling in love with the next random person they see (who’s no other than their fretful geography teacher, Miss Delavigne), Molly Manners’ infinitely witty debut unfolds cheekily around the high-stakes canvas of adolescence with great empathy and a droll sense of humor. Extraordinary newcomers Marni Duggan and Galaxie Clear are instant stars in this winsome coming-of-age tale for the ages, as proudly British as high tea, Shakespeare, and Jane Austen. Timeless and unmistakably authentic in its unique lens into girlhood, Extra Geography is a lasting addition to the growing canon movies about female friendships. —Tomris Laffly
films.producers: Sarah Brocklehurst

films.title: Fatherland
films.logline: Play Trailer Polish filmmaker Pawel Pawlikowski (MVFF41 Tribute) continues his ongoing examination of the emotional wounds and ruins of postwar Europe with this indelible drama. Joining the poetic ranks of his Oscar®-winning Ida (2013) and Oscar-nominated Cold War (MVFF41) in an unofficial trilogy, his latest black-and-white elegy traces the relationship between renowned writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his accomplished actress-writer daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller, among the finest performers working today), across a lyrical journey in a fractured Germany of 1949 where the exiled Mann is to receive the Goethe Prize. It’s the height of the Cold War, and the land that carries the duo’s roots is both deeply divided and consumed by unspoken guilt. A reflective and unforgettable study of identity, family, and national memory, Fatherland is simply a stunner in effortlessly braiding the makings of a classical road movie with an artistic statement on generational remorse. —Tomris Laffly
films.producers: Dimitri Rassam, Edward Berger, Ewa Puszczynska, Jeanne Tremsal, Lorenzo Gangarossa, Lorenzo Mieli, Mario Gianani

films.title: Fjord
films.logline: Play Trailer Winning his second Palme d’Or after 2007’s chilling masterwork 4 Months, 3 Weeks, and 2 Days , Romanian writer-director Cristian Mungiu delivers one of the most urgent movies of the year. And he does so through a query both timeless and of today: Is there a world in which we can be free of biases when pursuing truth and justice, or are we always a little blindsided by our belief systems? The audience will certainly wonder and self-interrogate in following Mungiu’s atmospheric legal thriller about a devout religious couple with ambiguous values (superstars Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan, both brilliant and against type) and their five children, disrupted by Norway’s inflexible child protection laws. An incisive courtroom procedural and a searing family drama that refreshingly checks all forms of moral pandering at the door, Mungiu’s latest is as cool, imposing, and silently deep as the fjord that lends this gorgeous enigma its backdrop. —Tomris Laffly

films.title: Giants Do Fall
films.logline: It’s a classic David vs. Goliath scenario: A group of fed-up, alarmed citizens, living on key stretches of land in Louisiana and Appalachia's Rust Belt where factory pollution and fracking have become de rigueur, square off against big business and politicos. The mobilized and impassioned group prove to be a formidable foe, demanding answers and accountability as they find themselves thrust into a role they never imagined they’d play: accidental activists. Giants Do Fall relates the devastating personal toll incurred by communities near petrochemical factories and fracking sites, and also how historical racism and corruption reflect another facet of these environmental disasters. Beyond that, Megan Ponder and Stiv Wilson’s documentary serves as an inspirational testament to the collective power and might ordinary citizens can wield when they unite around a common cause to protect what they cherish and hold dear. —Randy Myers

Two people come to his rescue: a middle-aged church musician who encourages him to play the organ, and a Huck Finn-like female schoolmate who teaches him to take risks and gives him his first hilariously unexpected kiss. Director Louis Clichy, an animator on Wall-E and Up , employs delicate hand-drawn watercolor imagery and casts his son Gary as Chrisophe’s voice, in this feature co-written with Frank Salome. Gabe Klinger finds humor, melancholy, and unexpected pleasures in Isabel's attempts to take control of her future, creating a warm and engaging portrait of a woman who keeps moving even when things don't go according to plan. Set in São Paulo's lively wine and restaurant scene, the city becomes an essential part of the story, captured on gorgeous, grainy 16mm film. Marina Person, who also collaborated on the screenplay, gives a wonderfully charismatic performance as Isabel, full of wit, determination, and humanity. With its great soundtrack, vibrant art direction, and love for life's imperfect pleasures, Isabel is an inviting toast to starting over. — João Federici

films.logline: Traveling through an overcrowded prison labyrinth in Douala, Cameroon, you’ll find a mercurial village full of petty thieves, murderers, and political scapegoats. A New Bell Prison ‘barker’ winds us through a chaotic din of bullies, hagglers, and sleepers, past guards pumping iron, into a closet-sized sanctuary where something magical happens. This is Jail Time Records, a music label founded by the film’s co-directors, former prisoner Steve Happi and his partner, Dione Roach. What began as an in-house recording studio is now a vital platform for artists—both incarcerated and free—using music to forge second chances amid poverty, corruption, and an overburdened judicial system. This directorial debut is unlike most prison documentaries, moving between the grit of daily survival and sudden bursts of rap, song, and dance, creating a shared stage of extraordinary expression. The label may not be able to engineer freedom from systemic failure, but it does offer hope for redemption and a different future for those who want it. The siblings relate stories of life at home in the family’s Brooklyn brownstone, their brother’s early interest in drawing, and the difficulties that arose when their parents separated. To augment these memories and catalog his rise in the art world, the film employs exceptional archival footage and key voices of contemporaries, including Fab 5 Freddy, Kenny Scharf, and Arthur Jafa. As these artists express what Basquiat meant to them and to the downtown NYC demimonde, Lisane and Jeanine speak to how affable, kind, gregarious, and flawed their sibling was. The result is very much a multidimensional portrait of the artist, but even more, the portrait of an endlessly fascinating man. The focus is on three kids—gorgeous rich-kid seducer James (Mitia Capellier-Audat), his charismatic but angry buddy Toni (Colas Quignard), and shy but observant nerdy outsider Suzanne (Suzanne Gerin) —and their teacher Mercier (Antonia Buresi). It’s hard to convey how subtle, mysterious, and completely intelligent this drama is—a dark but never dour or depressing investigation of the perils of adolescent fantasizing about sexual romance and family history, as well as the enduring effects of class antagonism and resentment. It’s a drama that conveys 2026’s complete sexual fluidity: Everyone is androgynous to a greater or lesser degree, and everyone is both promiscuous and frightened in unexpected ways. With marvelous sundrenched Italian landscapes photographed by Pierre Mazoyer and Atlan, a controlled ironic tone, and a superb ensemble. La Gradiva is one of the most assured directorial debuts in years. —Larry Gross

Her foundation is shaken by the sudden reappearance of Pinky, the sister-like childhood friend who abandoned Lady years ago and became a sex worker. Tempted by the promise of money, time with Pinky, and a possible path out of a nation on the brink of political and social combustion, Lady reluctantly accepts a job driving Pinky’s crew of glamorous, reckless coworkers through the dangerous netherworld of Lagos nightlife. Writer-director Nwosu, fresh among Africa’s new wave of auteurs, shines with her debut. The cast, which won the Special Jury Award for Acting Ensemble at Sundance, is phenomenal, crafting a moving portrayal of the unexpected sisterhood that finally breaches Lady’s armor. —D. Quinones

films.logline: The year is 2022 and the backdrop is Putin’s corruption-drenched Russia in LEVIATHAN Oscar-nominee Andrey Zvyagintsev’s latest, his first feature in a decade after 2017’s astounding LOVELESS. A bone-chilling reimagining of both Claude Chabrol’s LA FEMME INFIDELE and Adrian Lyne’s UNFAITHFUL, Zvyagintsev’s own thriller follows the essentials of the source material: amid various work pressures, a powerful businessman (Dmitriy Mazurov) learns that his increasingly distant wife (Iris Lebedeva) is cheating on him. But the filmmaker also puts a masterfully nihilistic spin on the story’s machinations, wondering, with his ingenious inquisitiveness and observantly still camerawork, if any authority in his motherland would care about unspeakable acts of crime when the country is at war with Ukraine, and a sense of lawlessness has seized the higher-ups. Together, they expose how technology, politics, and corporate decision-making fuel a digital culture where misogyny continues to thrive. Ultimately, the film amplifies the voices of women demanding accountability from governments and tech companies while safeguarding the future of the next generation of female leaders. —Michelle Svenson

films.logline: Play Trailer Elon Musk’s remarks—that it’s possible our contemporary reality is actually a computer simulated video game designed by a superior intelligence—inspired veteran filmmaker Alex Gibney in making this epic, four-hour documentary about the mercurial billionaire. Gibney focuses on Musk’s early success as a Silicon Valley start-up whiz and how he took financial control of Tesla while exaggerating his role in designing it, but also gives us the genuinely impressive story of the evolution of SpaceX. The darker side involves Musk’s brutally callous treatment of the many women who bore his children, and the way his paranoia about criminal liability drove him to become one of the most powerful power brokers in right-wing politics. When Gibney gets to the DOGE phase of Musk’s career and his alliance with Donald Trump, he confirms his starting thesis by demonstrating how the aesthetics of videogame reality are the best model for Musk’s approach to restructuring the United States government. Musk is now the wealthiest person in human history, and Gibney shows how the spreading influence of AI gives Musk unparalleled power to collect data on any and every person on this planet. This cumulative portrait of Elon Musk is dispassionate, mesmerizingly complex, and terrifying. —Larry Gross

films.logline: Play Trailer At the close of the five-and-a-half hour My Undesirable Friends: Part I—Last Air in Moscow , the last remaining holdouts of non-state news media in Russia were driven into exile. Already labeled “foreign agents,” harassed, jailed, and sometimes killed, they fled the country within days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. This likewise iPhone-shot, epic, and thrillingly urgent sequel records their fates since. The largely young female protagonists scatter first to Istanbul, then throughout Europe and beyond. Officially banned at home, stubbornly independent TV Rain persists in reaching millions of Russians from a new HQ in Latvia, even as constantly shifting politics imperil every refuge. Meanwhile, spies, threats, poisoning, further forced relocations, long-distance liquidation of personal assets, and other bitter pills constitute these brave colleagues’ reminders of “home.” Nonetheless, they keep reporting truths whose expression could exact the ultimate price...even as other nations (including our own) edge towards free-press crackdowns. —Dennis Harvey

films.title: Odyssey
films.logline: What if the United States hadn't pulled the plug on Apollo, as Apple's For All Mankind imagined? Built from 2,500 hours of restored archival footage, director Avi Belkin masterfully constructs a riveting thriller around the fateful Apollo 13 mission. Unfolding through the intimate perspective of astronaut Jim Lovell and his family, and executive produced by Tom Hanks, the film tracks his lunar dreams to that distressing message: "Houston, we've had a problem." Driven by a stark, chilling sci-fi score that pulsates from the vacuum of the cosmos to a frantic Mission Control, a united planet holds its breath as geopolitical divisions briefly recede—a fragile unity the real Apollo program wouldn't outlive. A country fractured by Vietnam, social unrest, anti-science sentiment, and mounting costs shuttered America's lunar program soon after Odyssey's splashdown. Half a century on, a new Space Race of global powers and private titans has turned our eyes back to the Moon, leaving us to ponder: What if we'd never stopped? -Michelle Svenson

At long last, Greaves’ son David completes his late father’s passion project, 50-year-old footage becoming 2026’s signature cinematic event. Once Upon a Time in Harlem is a tapestry of intimate, electric conversation between actors, writers, and others who helped shape the creative flowering of Black artists in the 1920s and ‘30s. But what’s remarkable—and also sobering—is how much of their exchanges touch on the racism and economic inequality still plaguing America in the 21st century. Much like the Oscar®-winning Summer of Soul , this nearly forgotten hangout brings history alive and emerges as a vital cultural landmark. It’s a party like no other—one full of brilliant personalities and bracing ideas. —Tim Grierson

In the film’s first movement, she faces two catastrophes, beginning with a doctor’s visit that reveals she’s suffering from early onset Alzheimer's. Rather than tell anyone, Mi-ja registers in an amateur poetry class. Then she discovers Jong-wook was among a group that raped a classmate, leading to her suicide. To keep the boys out of prison, a bribe must be paid to the victim’s poverty-stricken mother, but Mi-ja lacks the money to pay her share. As these two crises develop, she continues to work on writing a single poem. In lesser hands, all this could have easily turned into something overly sappy and cloying. But with his fifth feature, writer/director Lee Chang-dong eludes those risks, thanks to Yun’s luminous, often funny performance and his own uncanny gift for staging scenes with dispassionate, often wordless, subtlety. Both a lament for the frailty of human lives and a celebration of our insatiable appetite for creativity and beauty, Poetry is exquisite. —Larry Gross

films.logline: Play Trailer What happens when love is no longer enough to protect someone you care for? Amanda (Juliette Binoche), already struggling with her own life, finds herself at the center of an impossible family dilemma. Her mother Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall) is living with advanced dementia, while her devoted stepfather Martin (Tom Courtenay) refuses to accept that their intimate life must come to an end. When Amanda calls the authorities, a deeply private question becomes a matter for the police, carers, and institutions, setting the family on a path none of them can control. Sara (Florence Hunt), Amanda’s teenage daughter, brings another perspective as three generations of women navigate very different stages of love, desire, independence, and loss. Writer/director Lance Hammer handles this delicate subject with remarkable restraint, never offering easy answers or clear heroes or villains. The central trio finds humor, tenderness, frustration, and love in the smallest moments. Camping outside Mexico's National Palace, she waits for an audience with the country's first female president, carrying a question that has nagged at Lorena for years: What does justice look like when nothing can bring back your child? Lorena is among the directors of this documentary that transforms personal grief into a deeply intimate act of remembrance and resistance. The film moves between Lorena's recollections, her family's struggle, and the stories of other mothers who have also lost daughters to violence, creating a portrait that is as much about love and memory as it is about the search for accountability. Most importantly, Fátima emerges as no mere statistic, but as a girl with dreams, a daughter remembered with tenderness and determination. This triple Guadalajara International Film Festival award winner is a powerful testament to a mother who never imagined becoming an activist but found in that fight a way to keep her daughter's memory alive. - João Federici

films.logline: Play Trailer Filmmaking seems to run through Pegah Ahangarani’s veins. Her parents are both noted for their work behind the camera, while she’s been a screen actor since childhood, finding stardom at age 15 in 1999’s The Girl in the Sneakers . But in this unique decades-spanning nonfiction, the focus is not on professional history, but on the collision between personal and political spheres. Assembled entirely from preexisting footage and errata, it charts the often-cruel fates of immediate family, relatives, and mentors from before the 1979 Iranian Revolution—which many hoped would bring liberation—through successive crackdowns on dissent under the Islamic Republic. Some ultimately fled the country; others were less fortunate. Complete with harrowing glimpses from the midst of protests violently quelled by police, this first-person account laments a homeland that’s suffered under authoritarian control for the now-exiled director’s entire life. It’s a graceful tally of serial rebellions and disillusionments that won Cannes’ Golden Eye award this spring. —Dennis Harvey

films.logline: Play Trailer In the village, they call him a soldier, as well as an outsider and a misfit. Concealing many secrets and a facial scar, he excels at hard work in his quest to become part of the community. But beneath the soldier’s identity is a woman discovering a new sense of freedom and independence by living as a man, possibilities that would otherwise be denied to her. Sandra Hüller ( Anatomy of a Fall , MVFF46) delivers a performance of searing psychological intensity as a 17th-century war veteran. Markus Schleinzer’s third feature, after Michael and Angelo , is a stark historical drama; its striking black-and-white imagery reinforces its questions about gender, identity, and the price of belonging, revealing how simply being perceived as a man can open doors otherwise closed to women. Formally stunning and visually painterly, this human and deeply unsettling portrait turns a historical story into a provocative reflection on freedom, identity, and the lengths we go to claim our own lives. —Ivonne Cotorruelo

films.title: Árru
films.logline: Play Trailer In this inventive, visually arresting directorial debut from indigenous Sámi filmmaker Elle Sofe Sara, we follow Maia (Sara Marielle Gaup Beaska), a Sámi reindeer herder whose livelihood and ancestral lands are under imminent threat by an upcoming mining project. As a last-ditch effort, she contacts her estranged uncle for legal advice. But his return to their Sápmi home in Europe’s icy far north reopens deep familial wounds, and Maia faces an impossible choice of what to protect: her family or the land they rely upon to survive. The first ever feature film to do so, Árru weaves the joik , a traditional form of Sámi music, into the drama’s narrative, creating a singular, breathtaking audio-visual experience that brings Sámi culture to the big screen in a bold new way. —Sofia Felino

Friends and swimmers Paula and La Maestra navigate life with the same confidence they show in the pool. Dreams cast a quiet spell over the early stretches of the film, though its premonitory title, Sad Girlz , suggests that the girls’ carefree world will not remain untouched. One night when they go to a party, something happens to Paula. As their journey deepens and complicates their bond, these two remarkable young women provide a sense of warmth that makes Sad Girlz linger in the heart long after the credits roll. —Ivonne Cotorruelo MVFF49 Mind the Gap Creation Prize Winner

films.logline: “My mom is awesome!” exclaims young Sarah about her mom, Midge. From a daughter’s memories of her mother wielding her flashlight like a lightsaber as she vanquished nighttime demons lurking in Sarah’s bedroom; to winter walks in the Maine woods, stealing maple sap from the tree farm; through Sarah’s adolescence, coming out as queer, with Midge marching alongside her at LGBTQ+ rallies—awesomeness to the bone. Then things get tangled: small changes of behavior, easy to dismiss at first (“it’s just menopause”) until the signs are too evident to ignore. Leah Nelson’s beautifully rendered animated film, based on Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir ( Tangles: A Story About Alzheimer’s, My Mother and Me ), stars Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Samira Wiley, Bryan Cranston, Beanie Feldstein, Wanda Sykes, and Seth Rogen voicing Sarah’s lovingly tangled extended family, struggling to support each other as one of them slips away too fast. —KD Davis

Through visits with their diverse array of clients and Amy’s aging parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson), the two women grapple with precarious work-life balance, burnout, and many shades of heartbreak…but nothing a nice glass of wine can’t fix. Tender Loving Care is a powerful meditation on the nature of compassion: who we decide is deserving of care, if and how we can help those who refuse it, and the dear costs paid by those we expect to spend it freely. —Sofia Felino

With him is climbing partner Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), a Nepalese guide and veteran of expeditions to reach the top. Documentary filmmaker Jennifer Peedom’s ( Sherpa , Mountain ) first narrative feature relates the story of a loving husband and father who was never accepted by the European teams or the local Sherpa clans, but who navigated both cliques and cultures to become an essential element in achieving mountaineering’s greatest milestone. Amidst the epic Himalayan landscapes, every crevasse, every impossible face, and every blizzard presents a life-or-death scenario that Tenzing meets with patience, serenity, and love for the mountain in whose shadow he’s lived for decades. Willem Dafoe adds robust support as Colonel John Hunt, the head of the British expedition team. —Sterling Hedgpeth

films.title: The A-Word: The Future of Aging
films.logline: Play Trailer We’re all familiar with those slick hucksters hawking magical anti-aging elixirs they claim will extend lives and make us look and feel younger. Few, if any, work. Today, though, sees a new dawn emerging as vetted research scientists and innovators—some entrenched in the Bay Area—make significant breakthroughs that have the potential to add “quality” years to our lives. Greg Kohs, award-winning director of the 2008 documentary Song Sung Blue that inspired the 2025 Kate Hudson-Hugh Jackman film, explores exciting gains made in the biotech world and introduces us to groundbreakers making that happen, including San Francisco’s Celine Halioua, CEO/founder of a biotech startup that’s championing longevity medication that’s being tested on dogs. Kohs juxtaposes these encouraging developments with poignant testimonies from a close-knit community of residents in Maine whose stories suggest a positive outlook, an active lifestyle, and animal companions are key to making an extended lifespan worth living. —Randy Myers

How that came to be is only one element of Joanna Natasegara’s captivating documentary that is essentially two films in one: the story of that notorious CD and of the man who conceptualized the idea that an album could be treated as the rarest of fine art. The first half of the film relates how Dutch-Moroccan rapper/producer Tarik “Cilvaringz” Azzougarh—a longtime Wu-Tang Clan fan—found his way into their inner circle, while the second delves into how Once Upon a Time in Shaolin and its unique circumstances came to be. Wu-Tang Clan leader RZA executive produced this wildly entertaining film that benefits from having an irrepressible narrator in Cilvaringz, who treats his own life as the stuff of legend, and the collision of art and commerce that the Shaolin affair came to represent.

films.title: The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer
films.logline: Filmed over 25 years, this intimate documentary casts a tender and fearless eye over the lives of two inseparable cousins, Guillermina and Belinda, as they grow up in the rural Argentine Pampas. Celebrated photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti, in her prize-winning directorial debut, crafts a time capsule as fluid and heartrending as Boyhood and Seven Up! From carefree days playing dress-up and imagining vast futures, the girls mature before our eyes, dancing like no one is watching and ripening under the sun. In a blink, they tip into adulthood, effervescence fading under the weight of responsibility and narrowing options. Like a magic trick, though, their own daughters spring up to reclaim the joy of childhood as the camera keeps rolling. The heart of the narrative is the passage of time, but the film’s real power is how indelibly it captures women’s quiet resilience and the universal language of female friendship. Winner of the Filmmakers of the Present - Golden Leopard Award at the 2026 Locarno International Film Festival. —D. Quinones

films.title: The Last Place on Earth
films.logline: Play Trailer Deep in the breathtaking rainforests of Indonesia, an existential battle rages, to save Earth’s third-largest tropical rainforest from massive destruction caused by the palm oil boom, and with it, the future of the planet. This visually stunning, emotionally unsettling documentary captures the passion and purpose of Native people battling multinational corporations to save their homeland. Disturbing scenes reveal how illegal logging for the world’s most sought-after vegetable oil takes a devastating toll on lives and our planet’s climate. Filmed over nine years with a mostly Indonesian crew, David Booth Gardner captures activists overwhelmed by the race to save their lush jungles and endangered tigers, rhinos, elephants, and orangutans from smuggling, poaching, and the displacement of villagers, all under the watch of hovering drones. Inspiring and unnerving, this doc opens our eyes to these faraway battles, encouraging us all to lean in, speak up, and get involved in fighting corporate depredation for our global consumption. Executive produced by Louie Psihoyos ( The Cove ) and produced by the Oceanic Preservation Society. —Brendan Peterson

films.logline: Part slow-burn psychological thriller, part heart-wrenching family drama, The Liberation is filmmaker Guy Nattiv’s fictionalized portrayal of his grandmother’s life in the 1980s, and a visually lush deconstruction of the horrors of generational pain. Carrie Coon is at the top of her craft as Rita, a woman unravelling against the stress of her dead-end job, ever-demanding family, and the long-buried trauma she carries as a Holocaust survivor. When a chance encounter brings the free-spirited, charismatic Ricki (Lily James) into her orbit, Rita tastes the kind of freedom that life never afforded her through the all-female cult she steadily becomes a part of, cutting ties with her family as a result. While Rita’s teenage daughters (Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young) and her husband (Tracy Letts) see through the sinister undercurrents of Ricki’s tenets, they are woefully unprepared for the impossible task of rescuing a prisoner who doesn't want to be free. —Sofia Felino

films.title: The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd
films.logline: A relationship begins that pushes a couple down a rabbit hole of need, survival, promised freedom, and unexpected tragedy in writer/director Tim Blake Nelson’s powerful prison drama. Karen (Amanda Seyfried) volunteers as a creative writing teacher at the local penitentiary, a small window of escape from her abusive, unemployed, drunkard husband. Through reading the personal stories of the inmates, she forges an unexpected connection with one of them, Wilson Shedd (Scoot McNairy). Neither Karen nor Wilson are what they appear to be, and through Southern Gothic, nonlinear storytelling, the film peels the onions of their characters and hidden torments. Nelson (who also appears as the prison’s warden) does not just deliver a tale of two haunted souls but also provides a steely eyed, unblinkered gaze on capital punishment. The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd is a potent film that address real-world issues with compassion, poignancy, and vividness. —Sterling Hedgpeth

films.title: The Man I Love
films.logline: Play Trailer In late 1980s New York, Jimmy (Rami Malek), a theater artist living with AIDS, throws himself back into his work, rehearsing a new stage production while surrounded by lovers, family, friends, and fellow artists. Ira Sachs brings us into a world where fear and extraordinary creative energy exist side by side, capturing a generation determined to keep making art, falling in love, having sex, laughing, and living. Rather than turning the AIDS crisis into a conventional illness story, Sachs finds its presence in the relationships, silences, bodies, and choices of the people who lived through it. Malek gives Jimmy a magnetic, mercurial presence, while Tom Sturridge, Rebecca Hall, and Luther Ford bring intimacy, affection, and shifting loyalties into his world. Music becomes another language, with performances revealing what Jimmy cannot always say. Following Peter Hujar’s Day (MVFF48), Sachs returns to New York with a deeply sensual portrait of art, desire, community, and survival. —João Federici

films.title: El Deshielo
films.logline: Play Trailer The year is 1992, and the backdrop is Chile’s transition from Pinochet to democracy. In her long-awaited sophomore feature, director Manuela Martelli ( Chile ‘76 , MVFF45) returns to the country's disappeared, spinning out a political allegory through the perspective of nine-year-old Inés (Maya O’ Rourke), the story consistently framed at her eye level. A ski resort owned by Ines’s grandmother gleams against the frozen Andes. In grainy footage, an iceberg traverses the Atlantic Ocean and the screen, bound to a grandiose yet reluctant promise to remain unmelted. With an icy formal elegance, Martelli turns the shrill scrape of skis against snow into an eerie accomplice to Inés, after a guest's disappearance forces the child into the adults’ pact of silence. This Cannes premiere is unnerving, like the immaculate white landscape that surrounds it—a world beginning to thaw but still holding much of the iceberg that lies beneath its surface. —Ivonne Cotorruelo

films.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
films.logline: Play Trailer It’s hard out there for an aging pickpocket like Harry (a flawless John Turturro in an instantly iconic coat), an analog man facing a digital world where people no longer carry cash. Gracing the streets of New York with his traditional elegance, Harry finds a kindred spirit in his partner-in-crime Ben (Steve Buscemi), and lovingly cares for his nonverbal wife, before he accidentally antagonizes the wrong sort: the spoiled scion (Will Price) of a crime family. In sending Harry on a five-borough odyssey to salvage the situation, Noah Segan’s elegiac knockout gently mourns the adrift qualities of a bygone era, while romantically portraying the city’s diverse communities that our desperate, GPS-less protagonist relies on for acts of kindness. There is poetry in Segan’s mournfully textured lens, accompanied by jazzy beats and timeless Big Apple ballads. A love letter to one of cinema’s favorite towns, Segan’s unassuming character study joins the ranks of great NYC movies. —Tomris Laffly

films.title: The Unrooted Bloom
films.logline: Alongside co-director Cassidy Friedman (Voices Beyond the Wall, Circles), visionary Bay Area poet, educator, and community activist Amber Allen-Peirson turns the camera on her own life in this deeply moving quest for belonging. A biracial woman living in Marin County, Allen-Peirson grapples with the complexities of her identity—of the nuances of living as a person with both Black and white roots in a nation founded on division. Using poetry to narrate a striking collage of archival footage and vérité moments from her present, Allen-Peirson deftly captures the ways in which she’s pulled in an overwhelming number of directions in her personal and professional lives. Torn between carrying on a legacy of fighting for what she believes in and simply trying to exist in an ever-demanding world, Allen-Peirson demonstrates that belonging can bloom through a life examined—in the pursuit of clarity. —Kate Bove

films.title: This Bright Light
films.logline: Play Trailer Tamarin Luchessa seemed destined to burn brightly. An Olympic-bound rhythmic gymnast, her course was derailed by a diabetes diagnosis as a teenager. Her life became marked by medical crises, personal struggles, and eventually a kidney and pancreas transplant that altered her personality in ways even her family and friends could not recognize—only for her original self to return when the organs later began to fail. Sonoma County filmmaker Alexandra Lexton ( Fools’ Paradise (lost?) , MVFF47; The Lure of This Land , MVFF42) follows Tamarin’s mother, Cindy, from the mysteries of cellular memory into more ethereal terrain, where mediums, intuitives, and signs from beyond suggest our connections may extend past the physical body. Moving between science and spirit, this deeply personal docudrama chronicles a mother-daughter pact to help others, offering a loving reflection on life and death. —Michelle Svenson

In the film’s memorable ensemble, Mildred is played with unbridled cynicism and priceless, profane sarcasm by the inimitable Frances McDormand. She’s an inconsolable grieving mother with a triple-billboard-sized grudge and a fathomless rage demanding to be reckoned with. The ones doing the reckoning are the local police force: the beloved but ineffective Chief Willoughby (Woody Harrelson) and his hotheaded junior officer Dixon, a dimwitted, heavy-drinking momma's boy with a penchant for brutality, notably played by Sam Rockwell (MVFF49 Tributee and Oscar® winner for this performance)—with both hilarious and incendiary consequences. British playwright-turned-film-maker Martin McDonagh ( Seven Psychopaths , MVFF35; Wild Horse Nine , MVFF49 Opening Night) brings his singular brand of violence and black humor to this renegade masterpiece that surprises at every turn. But one thing remains constant: Hell definitely hath no fury like a Mildred Hayes ignored. Just ask Officer Dixon. —Joanne Parsont

films.title: threeASFOUR: FULL CIRCLE
films.logline: From Björk to Chloë Sevigny to Meredith Monk, the New York City-based fashion collective threeASFOUR has dressed some of the world’s most avant-garde fashionistas in singular looks that blend nature and technology. While some write off runway couture as frivolous or banal, the visionary minds at threeASFOUR know that the human body is an endlessly fascinating art medium—something they prove time and again with their prescient designs. But as s the film points out, there are “certain things that get attention, [and] certain things that sell,” and for a fashion collective that favors vision and collaboration over all else that can prove challenging, especially in a multibillion-dollar industry that demands profit and favors easy, trend-making replication. Directed by Sean Ono Lennon and co-directed by Brian Gonzalez, this behind-the-scenes doc follows threeASFOUR co-founders Gabi Asfour, Angela Donhauser, and Adi Gil over several years as they pursue creative freedom and work that inspires unity. —Kate Bove

films.title: Union Town
films.logline: Two-time Best Documentary Feature Oscar® winner Barbara Kopple nabbed her first in 1976 for Harlan County, USA , which chronicled Kentucky coal miners’ bitter but ultimately successful strike for better working conditions. 1990’s American Dream was less upbeat: Threatened with pay cuts or no jobs at all, Minnesota meatpacking-plant workers found a decade of Reaganomics had thoroughly weakened their bargaining power. Decades later, the director’s focus is a whole new labor sector as she completes the trilogy she began 50 years ago. Those who serve UPS, Amazon, and apps like Door Dash deliver 2.4 million packages every day within NYC alone. Many aren’t official employees but third-party contractors sans benefits or job protection, their toil frequently underpaid, exhausting, sometimes downright dangerous. Meanwhile, the corporations themselves make astronomical profits. Can unions, activism, and strikes still secure livable wages, among other basics that are rapidly disappearing for many in the 21st century? Full of real-life drama and compelling personalities, Kopple’s latest is a true sign of our times. —Dennis Harvey

films.title: When a Witness Recants
films.logline: With her trademark command of complex social issues and deeply human storytelling, veteran documentarian Dawn Porter (John Lewis: Good Trouble ) examines the Harlem Park Three—teenagers wrongfully sentenced to life in prison for the 1983 murder of a Baltimore middle schooler. Inspired by Jennifer Gonnerman’s New Yorker reporting, the investigative documentary tracks how police coerced 13 and 14-year-old witnesses into fabricating testimony, and how the state's case collapsed 36 years later in 2019, when those same witnesses formally recanted. Interweaving archival footage, graphic novel-style animation, and tense legal depositions, the film moves past the courtroom to capture the profound emotional toll on the trio, boys who became men behind bars, separated from their families and the world outside. Exploring the possibility of reconciliation between the exonerated and a key childhood witness, Porter ultimately asks what justice, accountability, and healing can look like in the wake of America's longest combined wrongful conviction. —Michelle Svenson

films.title: Where the Silence is Heard
films.logline: Play Trailer Gabriela Pena and Picho García’s deeply personal documentary delves into what isn’t expressed—the silences, unspoken fears, and absences that shape both Pena’s family history and her relationship with her mother. At the film’s outset, Pena moves to Valparaíso, the Chilean port city her family was forced from decades earlier amid the Pinochet regime. While reconnecting with her grandparents, the filmmaker takes on the formidable project of renovating the now-dilapidated house her family left behind. As she strips the former home to its core, Pena also digs into her relationship with her mother and how the physical distance between them could actually be a means of getting closer. Beautifully lensed and rivered by personal memories and archival footage, this achingly intimate family portrait explores how intergenerational trauma shapes how we love, all as one woman attempts to find peace before a new generation joins the story. —Kate Bove

films.title: Wicker
films.logline: Play Trailer Playing to the peak of their immaculate powers, Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, and Peter Dinklage bring grand charm, delight, and whimsy to this altogether unique and fantastical folk romance for the ages. Mocked by the eccentric, coupled townsfolk for her spinsterish manner, a fisherwoman (Colman) in this medieval world that is both wonderful and strange beseeches the local basket maker (Dinklage) to weave her a husband. He does, bringing to life the wicker man (Skarsgård) of her dreams, creating a cascading sensation throughout the village. Lushly designed, carefully crafted, and skillfully paced, this adaptation of Ursula Willis’s beguiling short story generated its own percolating buzz when it premiered at Sundance. Husband-and-wife directing duo Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson imbue their fractured tale with the liveliness and wit of master storytellers, weaving their mythical yarn with precision and captivating magic that is all too rare. —Landon Zakheim

films.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
films.logline: Play Trailer Academy Award® winner Mahershala Ali's turn as a devout Muslim who quietly makes his living as a professional killer headlines this elevated blend of exemplary action, taut thriller and moving drama resulting in a stunning work. In writer-director Bassam Tariq’s stirring fable, Ali’s Latif returns from his latest murder to a family in crisis and grief. Mourning the loss of his wife, Latif is left to care for his three children, including a newborn in desperate need of breast milk, while facing judgment from his community, pressure from a dangerous colleague, and the wrath of a potential new target, a fundamentalist gun-toting Christian zealot played by a sublime John Cho. Bolstered by a muscular directorial vision and impactful performances, Tariq’s emotional tale of vengeance, honor, and family offers incredible sweep and stunning skill that will linger in the bones and the soul. —Landon Zakheim
